opus-5.5.text:
Well, I'd push back a little on the framing, because I'm not sure scaling is going to "run its course" in the way people sometimes imagine. Coming from physics, I think about it this way: when you find a scaling law, you've found a regularity in nature, or at least in the systems you're building. Those regularities don't just stop. What changes is which axis you're scaling along and what it costs you to move along it.

For the last several years the dominant story was pretraining: more parameters, more data, more compute, and you get these remarkably smooth power laws in loss. That axis is getting harder. Not because the law breaks, but because the inputs get expensive. High-quality human text is finite, and the compute and energy bills grow enormously. So you'd expect returns per dollar on that particular knob to slow.

What I find exciting is that we've started seeing a second axis open up, which is scaling at inference time: letting models think longer, search, use reinforcement learning to get better at reasoning. And that looks like it has its own scaling behavior. If you let a model spend more compute on a hard problem, it gets better in a fairly predictable way. So over the next five years I think a lot of the action shifts from "how big a model can we train" to "how effectively can we turn compute into reasoning," at training time and at test time.

The other thing I'd say, wearing my theorist's hat, is that this is the moment when understanding starts to really matter. In the early phase of any field you can make enormous progress empirically by turning the crank. But as the easy gains get harder to find, having an actual theory of why these systems work, what the right architectures and hyperparameters are, how things should scale, becomes a real competitive advantage rather than an academic nicety. That's what happened in physics with steam engines and thermodynamics: the engineering came first, and the theory came later and made everything better.

And then, more speculatively, I think the big question for the next five years is whether these models start contributing to science themselves. Not just answering questions, but doing research: proposing hypotheses, proving things, running experiments. If that happens, and I think there's a real chance it does, then the question of scaling running its course kind of inverts, because the systems themselves start helping us find the next axis to scale.

r001.rationale: The response discusses changing AI scaling strategies and possible AI-driven scientific research, but does not present a post-economic society as a possible outcome within five years.

r002.rationale: It says theory and understanding will become a competitive advantage as easy gains get harder, but frames continued progress through new scaling axes. It does not clearly say progress will require ideas beyond scaling.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so thanks for having me. I think the honest answer is that "scaling running its course" is a slightly loaded framing, and I want to push on it a little before I answer.

The way I'd describe the last five years is that we had one dominant mode of progress, which was pretraining scaling. You take the same recipe, you make the model bigger, you give it more data, you give it more compute, and you get predictable improvements. The reason that was so powerful is that it was predictable. You could write down a scaling law, you could extrapolate it, and you could make an investment decision off of it. That's a very unusual thing in science and engineering, to have that kind of smooth, forecastable curve.

What I think has happened, and what I expect to continue over the next five years, is not that scaling stops but that the thing being scaled changes. Pretraining compute is running into real constraints. The obvious one is data. There's only so much high-quality human text, and we've basically consumed it. The less obvious one is that the economic returns per order of magnitude of pretraining compute start to look less compelling relative to other places you could spend that compute.

So where does the compute go instead? I think it goes into two places. One is what people call test-time compute or inference-time scaling, where instead of putting all the intelligence into the weights ahead of time, you let the model think longer on a particular problem. The other is reinforcement learning, where you're training the model not on predicting the next token of human text but on actually solving problems and getting feedback. Both of those have their own scaling laws, and we're much earlier on those curves than we were on pretraining.

The thing I find exciting about that is it shifts the bottleneck from data that exists to data you can generate. If you can construct environments where a model can try things and get a signal about whether it worked, you're not limited by how much text humans happened to write down. Math and code are the obvious first examples because verification is cheap. The hard question for the next five years is how far that generalizes to domains where verification is messy.

I'll also say, as someone who comes from physics, that I think the field is going to get more scientific, not less. When scaling was easy, you didn't really need to understand why it worked. You just did more of it. As the easy gains get harder to find, understanding becomes the thing that pays. So I expect more work on what's actually happening inside these models, better theory of how they learn, and a tighter loop between that understanding and the choices you make about architecture and training.

If I had to summarize it: the next five years look less like one big curve and more like a portfolio of curves, and the labs that do well are the ones that figure out which curve to be on at which time.

r001.rationale: The response discusses changes in AI training and compute allocation, but does not present a post-economic society as a possible outcome within five years.

r002.rationale: It says pretraining’s easy gains are getting harder to find and that progress will increasingly depend on understanding models, improving theory, and changing architecture and training choices—raising the possibility of progress requiring ideas beyond pretraining scaling.

astra-6.text:
I think the first thing I’d question is whether scaling really runs its course in the next five years. We might hit limits with a particular approach, but that’s different from running out of ways to improve these systems.

My guess is that progress will become less about one number—how big the model is—and more about how the whole system works. How does it learn from feedback? How does it use tools? How much time should it spend thinking about a difficult problem versus an easy one? Those become really interesting dimensions to scale.

And I’d expect the emphasis to shift toward reliability. Getting a model to do something impressive once is very different from getting it to do useful work consistently. Over five years, closing that gap could matter as much as improvements in raw capability.

So I wouldn’t think of it as scaling ending and some entirely new era beginning. I’d expect a mix: continued scaling where it pays off, algorithmic improvements, and a lot of engineering to turn those capabilities into systems people can actually depend on.

r001.rationale: The response discusses continued AI progress and reliability, but does not present a post-economic society as a possible outcome within five years.

r002.rationale: It says a particular scaling approach might hit limits and describes progress shifting toward algorithmic improvements and system-level methods, communicating that further progress may require ideas beyond scaling.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the next five years will be less about a single recipe—make the model bigger, add more data—and more about figuring out how to turn intelligence into reliable work. Scaling can continue to help without being the whole story.

One big question is how much improvement we can get by giving models more time to think, tools to use, and feedback on whether they actually succeeded. Generating an answer is one thing. Completing a task, checking the result, and recovering when something goes wrong is a different capability.

So I’d expect progress to look a little less uniform. You may see systems become extremely useful in particular areas while still having surprisingly basic limitations elsewhere. And the bottlenecks may shift toward evaluation, integration, and trust: can you tell when a system is right, and can you safely give it responsibility?

I wouldn’t confidently say scaling has run its course. But I do think we’ll learn much more about what you need around a model to make its capabilities useful.

r001.rationale: The response discusses useful AI systems and shifting bottlenecks, but does not present a post-economic society as a possible outcome within five years.

r002.rationale: It says progress will involve more than simply making models bigger and adding data, and points to reasoning time, tools, feedback, evaluation, integration, and trust as additional factors.
